headline: Moriches Inlet's West Cut Deepened Two Feet This Month — And the Bass Know It
subhead: A scoured channel edge off Cupsogue is funneling bait and stripers on the outgoing tide, while fluke pick up steam through the throat.
body_markdown:
I ran a depth check off the west jetty at Cupsogue on Wednesday's low and the sounder told me something I'd been suspecting for two weeks — the channel edge that runs along the old core has scoured out another two feet since the June full moon tides. We're looking at 18 to 20 feet now in the throat where it used to hold 15 to 16, and the sand that came out of there has piled onto the bar east of the cut, the one that used to be barely a foot proud at dead low. That's classic Moriches behavior — this inlet doesn't sit still, it never has since '92 when the last big realignment happened, and every strong ebb this summer has been carving the west side a little harder while building the east flank. For anglers that matters because current speed through a deepened cut increases, and increased current means bait gets funneled instead of scattered. That's exactly what's setting up the bass bite right now.

Stripers have been working that west edge hard on the second half of the outgoing, stacking on the current seam where the deep water meets the shallower flat that runs off Pattersquash. I had a report of slot fish to 32 inches taken there Monday evening on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, just outside the wash where the rip folds back on itself. If you're throwing artificials, a 1.5-ounce bucktail in white or chartreuse, cast up-current and allowed to swing down through the seam before you start your retrieve, has been the better producer than anything worked cross-current. The fish are sitting tight to that edge, not roaming the flat, so you need to put the lure right on the seam or you're wasting casts. Night tide, same location, eels have taken a few bigger fish — nothing over 20 pounds that I've heard of, but enough overslot activity to keep guys coming back after dark.

Bluefish have been running in with the bass on the same tide stage, and they're not small — snapper-class fish are still around the docks in the back bay, but out at the inlet you're seeing 3- to 6-pound choppers blitzing on peanut bunker pushed out of the bay on the ebb. Metal — a Hopkins or a Kastmaster in the 1-ounce range — worked fast through the froth has been the ticket. Nothing subtle needed there.

Fluke fishing has actually been the pleasant surprise of the last two weeks. The bite that's been building across the South Shore inlets — Shinnecock, Reynolds Channel, and here — has real legs to it now. I'm marking fish holding on the sand-to-mud transition just inside the inlet mouth, roughly 14 to 18 feet, where the current slows enough for them to sit and ambush but stays clean enough that they're feeding actively. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the boat working the edge of the channel, have produced keeper-class fish to 22 inches. The key has been timing the drift to the last two hours of the ebb — once the tide goes fully slack the fish seem to shut down until the current builds again on the new flood.

Weakfish have shown in smaller numbers than I'd like to report — a few nice fish in the 20-inch class taken on bucktail tipped with squid strips around the marsh edges near Tuthill Point, fished at night on the last of the outgoing. It's not the consistent bite we saw a few Junes back, but it's there if you're willing to put in dark hours and cover the grass edges quietly.

Offshore, the ocean off the inlet mouth is running a moderate southeast swell — 2.3 feet at a 10-second period according to the nearest buoy reading — which is enough texture to keep the surf at Cupsogue interesting without blowing it out. Water out there is sitting in the low 70s, which tells me the bass holding tight to the beach are doing so more for bait than temperature comfort; the real cool water is still offshore or trapped in the deeper cuts of the inlet itself. That's part of why the inlet edges are outproducing the open beach right now — cooler, faster water concentrated in one lane beats warm, slow water spread over a mile of sand.

Porgies are around the deeper holes inside the bay on standard high-low rigs with clam, nothing spectacular but steady if you need a bend in the rod with the kids. Blackfish are still mostly off-limits behavior-wise this time of year — a few juvenile fish showing around the rocks at the jetty tips, but I wouldn't target them seriously until fall structure fishing kicks back in.

Looking ahead, if the swell holds in this 2- to 3-foot range and doesn't build past it, I'd keep working that scoured west channel edge on the outgoing through the coming week — the current there is doing the work of concentrating bait for you. If a bigger blow rolls through and reshapes that bar again, and it's due given how active this inlet's been all season, I'd expect the fish to shift with it fast, probably sliding onto whatever new edge forms. That's the nature of fishing a system that never stops rebuilding itself. Watch the bar, not the calendar.
